1 – Stand upright with your feet hip-width apart. 2 – Focus your eyes on one point. 3 – Lift one leg so that your foot is no longer touching the floor. 4 – Maintain your balance for as long as possible. Stop the timer as soon as the raised foot touches the floor. Repeat the test with each leg and record your best result. A large difference between the two legs may indicate a trainable difference. What the single-leg stance test shows: Under the described eyes-open conditions, this test provides a guide to your static balance and coordination. Regular practice can help improve balance and make everyday movements safer. The test does not replace a medical assessment.

Knowing about cancer and cardiovascular disease in your family enables targeted preventive care. If you know your family history, you can address personal risk factors early and support early detection through appropriate screening.

Exercises that strengthen the muscles using weights, equipment or your own body weight (e.g. push-ups, squats or weight training). WHO recommendation: At least twice a week for all major muscle groups.
On how many days per week do you do strength training?

1 – Lie face down with your hands beneath your shoulders. 2 – Straighten your arms and lift your body off the floor. 3 – Keep your body, hips and legs in a straight line. 4 – Lower your body until your chest almost touches the floor. 5 – Push back up to the starting position. Repeat without a break until you cannot continue. What the push-up test shows: Push-ups measure the strength of your chest, shoulders, arms and core. Strong upper-body muscles are important for everyday activities such as carrying or getting up and help prevent injuries from falls.

Omega-3 fatty acids from marine sources support your brain and heart and have a strong anti-inflammatory effect throughout the body. Because the body cannot produce enough of them itself, it is important to obtain them regularly through food. Algal oil is an excellent vegan alternative to fish. Your body can use it directly, unlike omega-3 precursors from other plant oils.
How often per week do you eat oily fish (e.g. salmon, mackerel or herring) or take an omega-3 supplement?

Vegetables & salads: spinach, broccoli, carrots, tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, onions, garlic Fruit: apples, bananas, berries, oranges, grapes, avocado Grains & pseudograins: oats, quinoa, millet, buckwheat, barley, brown rice Seeds: chia seeds, linseeds, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, sesame seeds Legumes & nuts: lentils, chickpeas, beans, almonds, walnuts Spices & herbs: basil, oregano, turmeric, ginger, cinnamon, pepper Mushrooms: button mushrooms, shiitake, oyster mushrooms Why is plant diversity important? A colourful variety of plants provides nutrients, antioxidants and fibre. Each plant contains its own bioactive compounds that support different functions in the body. Diversity particularly supports the gut microbiome and thereby promotes a healthy intestinal flora.
What counts as a plant food, for example?
How many different plant foods did you eat in the past week?

This question assesses how regularly you include sources of protein. It does not calculate how many grams of protein you actually consume per day and per kilogram of body weight. Suitable sources of protein include: • Legumes such as lentils, beans or chickpeas • Tofu, tempeh, eggs, quark, yoghurt or cottage cheese • Fish or meat Guidance for regular strength training: For healthy adults, around 1.4–1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is a practical guide. In a large meta-analysis, the average additional benefits for building lean mass levelled off markedly from around 1.6 g/kg/day. This is not a strict biological limit. Up to around 2.0 g/kg/day may be appropriate on an individual basis during very high training loads or a deliberate energy deficit. Most people do not need this amount, and age alone is not a reason to aim for 2.0 g/kg/day. Strength training provides the training stimulus; protein provides the building blocks. Protein powder is not automatically necessary. People under the age of 18 and those with kidney disease or a medically prescribed diet should discuss the appropriate amount with a healthcare professional.
What does this question measure, and how much is appropriate?
How often do you manage to include a clear source of protein in at least three meals or snacks spread throughout the day (e.g. legumes, tofu, eggs, dairy products, fish or meat)?

Stopping smoking is worthwhile at any age. After just one day, irritation of the airways begins to decrease; within a few months, circulation and lung function improve. After about one year, the risk of coronary heart disease is approximately half that of someone who continues to smoke. Your sense of smell also recovers, food tastes better and you feel more capable.
Do you smoke, or have you smoked in the past? (e.g. cigarettes, vapes or shisha)
How often do you feel full for around four hours after your main meals, without wanting a snack?

Long periods of sitting or lying down, excluding sleep, increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Even a short break every hour, such as standing up, stretching, walking a few steps or taking the stairs, significantly reduces this risk.

How many hours do you spend sitting or lying down on a typical day? (e.g. at work or in education, while eating, travelling, using media, during leisure or while relaxing, but excluding sleep and naps)
Social media can be addictive and can affect both mental and general health. Potential effects include sleep problems, depression, anxiety and social conflict.
Do you spend more time on social media than you would like?

Someone who has fallen once has a high risk of falling again. Falls are therefore among the most common health risks in older age. A single fall can substantially affect independence and quality of life because of injuries. The good news is that targeted balance, strength and mobility training can significantly reduce the risk.
How confident do you feel during everyday movements? (e.g. getting up from the floor, walking on forest paths or stepping down from a stool)
Do you become short of breath when you climb two flights of stairs?

• Ready meals, frozen pizza • Sweets, biscuits, crisps • Soft drinks, energy drinks • Sausages and processed meat • White bread, sweet baked goods Practical rule: More than five ingredients or names that are difficult to pronounce usually indicate a highly processed product. Why are processed foods problematic? Many highly processed products contain a lot of sugar, salt, less favourable fats and additives while lacking fibre and important nutrients. Not every processed food is equally problematic. The key is to reduce the proportion of highly processed products and gradually include more fresh, nutrient-rich foods in everyday life.
How often do you choose highly processed foods in a typical week?
I feel accepted and included by the people around me.

High blood pressure often goes unnoticed but is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Depending on your age, lifestyle or family history, it may also be worthwhile to assess your personal risk of cancer or early signs of type 2 diabetes. Identifying risks early and making small changes in daily life can reduce both the risks and their effects.
Have you learned about conditions such as cancer, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes and had your personal risk assessed?

1 – Place your back and pelvis fully against a straight wall. 2 – Position your feet parallel and approximately hip-width apart. 3 – Slide down until your hips and knees form an angle of approximately 90°. 4 – Distribute your weight evenly across both legs. Do not support your legs or brace against the wall with your hands or arms. 5 – Continue to breathe normally and hold the position for as long as possible. First do a short practice attempt and then one timed attempt. Start the timer when you are in the correct position. End the test as soon as your pelvis or back loses contact with the wall, you slide noticeably upwards or you use your hands for support. Stop if you experience pain, dizziness or shortness of breath. What the wall-sit test shows: It measures the local muscular endurance of your legs and gluteal muscles. These muscles are important for stability, mobility and safety. Training them helps you remain active, mobile and independent for longer.
How to perform the wall-sit test correctly
